name: JAX
summary: A Python numerical computing system that represents array programs through functional transformations, traces them into jaxprs, lowers compiled computations to XLA, and assigns arrays to devices through explicit sharding objects.

features.name: Functional transformation composition
features.description: JAX exposes transformations such as jit, grad, jacfwd, jacrev, vmap, and pmap that take functions or array programs and produce transformed callable computations. The API implementation composes these transformations through tracing and vector-Jacobian or batching machinery rather than requiring users to construct a separate graph format.
benefits: Reuses one Python function across differentiation, batching, and compilation workflows
Keeps transformation selection at the callable boundary
costs: Transformation semantics require side-effect-free code and compatible traced control flow
Nested transformations can increase compilation and debugging complexity

features.name: Tracer and jaxpr intermediate representation
features.description: During tracing, JAX wraps arguments in tracer objects that record JAX primitive operations; make_jaxpr exposes a Jaxpr containing variables, equations, effects, and typed abstract values. Python side effects are not represented in the jaxpr.
benefits: Makes a compact, inspectable computation representation available before lowering
Supports transformation-specific interpretation of primitive operations
costs: Python effects can occur during tracing without appearing in the representation
Value-dependent Python control flow may fail or require JAX control-flow primitives

features.name: Explicit lowering and XLA compilation boundary
features.description: JAX jit traces a function, lowers the resulting computation, compiles it through XLA, and reuses compiled code for compatible later calls; the AOT API exposes separate trace, lower, and compile stages.
benefits: Allows whole-function optimization and accelerator execution
Separates Python tracing from compiled executable reuse
costs: Initial calls pay tracing and compilation costs
Static argument changes and shape or dtype changes can trigger additional compilations

features.name: Array sharding and device placement
features.description: JAX arrays carry a sharding object that maps global array indices to devices; Array and Shard APIs expose global shape, device indices, replica identifiers, and local shard data. This makes placement part of the array execution contract.
benefits: Represents replicated and partitioned data with one array abstraction
Provides explicit placement information for multi-device execution
costs: Programs must satisfy sharding and addressability constraints
Data movement and replicated storage add communication or memory cost

mathematical_views.question: How do function transformations compose into differentiated, batched, and compiled computations?
assumptions: A program is represented as a pure callable over pytrees of array-like values
Each transformation has a compatible interpreter over JAX primitives
The view abstracts backend-specific lowering details

mathematical_views.question: Which primitive equations and abstract values are produced by tracing a callable?
assumptions: Nodes are typed variables or primitive equations
Tracing observes JAX operations but not arbitrary Python side effects
The graph is a representation of a traced specialization, not all possible Python executions

mathematical_views.question: When does a callable transition from Python execution to a cached accelerator executable?
assumptions: Trace and compilation are keyed by relevant argument properties and static values
Lowering preserves the computation needed by the selected backend
Cache reuse does not imply semantic equivalence across all shapes and devices

mathematical_views.question: How are global array indices partitioned or replicated across devices?
assumptions: A sharding defines a device-to-index relation for a global shape
The model abstracts collective operations and transport implementation

benefits: One callable can serve multiple numerical execution strategies
costs: Purity and transformation compatibility constrain ordinary Python idioms

benefits: Inspectability and interpreter reuse before backend compilation
costs: Trace-time behavior differs from ordinary eager Python behavior

benefits: Optimized accelerator execution and executable reuse
costs: Compilation latency and cache specialization consume time and resources
Sharding constraints and communication complicate program design
